claims.text: A controlled mild reduction heat treatment promotes surface segregation in a near-equiatomic, multi-principal automotive alloy catalyst.
Reduction-induced surface segregation simultaneously enhances low-temperature oxidation activity, poisoning resistance, and long-term durability without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
A FeCoNiCu-based composition is an example of a near-equiatomic, multi-principal starting catalyst for this intervention.
Treatment in dilute H2/Ar at a moderate temperature can drive surface segregation while avoiding sintering.
The treatment forms surface-segregated phases enriched in catalytically active sites.
Mild reduction alters the local chemical environment at the catalyst surface through controlled elemental segregation.
Modification of the local structure and chemical environment of active sites can lower reaction barriers and accelerate reactions on high-entropy-material surfaces.
The segregated surface provides more accessible oxidation-active sites.
The altered surface is more resistant to poisoning by H2O and NO.
The mild reduction treatment mitigates sintering and structural degradation during prolonged thermal stress.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the treated catalyst will have lower light-off temperatures for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation, with light-off below 150 °C.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the treated catalyst will retain more activity during exposure to H2O and NO.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the treated catalyst will show improved durability over accelerated aging cycles.
The predicted benefits apply under transient low-temperature exhaust conditions and simulated long-term aging.
Excessive treatment temperature or duration may cause sintering or adverse phase transformations that eliminate the benefits.
The optimal reduction temperature, duration, and H2 concentration, as well as the detailed segregation dynamics, remain unresolved.
The intervention can be tested against an untreated control under identical transient-exhaust, H2O/NO exposure, and accelerated-aging conditions.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in activity, poisoning resistance, and durability, or observation of deleterious sintering or degradation, would falsify the hypothesis.
